title: Celsus and Hierocles: lesser powers honored so that the supreme God is never left
source_text: LXXV. Unde est quod Celsus apud Origenem affirmat Eum qui plures Deos veneratur, hoc ipso in quantum unum aliquem Deo maximo subditum colit, rem gratam summo Deo facere: & addit, Quod neminem honore prosequi licet, nisi quem ille honorari vult: quapropter qui veneretur ejus subditos non offendere illum cujus omnes sunt. Ideoque sic coli vult inferiores illas sub summo Deo potestates, Ut Deus nullo pacto unquam relinquatur, non noctu, non interdiu, non in privato, non in publico, non in cogitationibus ullis, non in operibus, sed sive cum his, sive sine his semper intenta sit ad Deum anima. Et postea, Sic, inquit, magnum Deum magis venerari videberis, si hos quoque hymnis honores & laudibus. Quibus consonum est quod docet Hierocles, Deos ita agnoscendos & colendos, ut sunt ab authore suo & parente distincti, non autem eorum dignitatem supra modum esse attollendam; denique cultum esse referendum ad eorum opificem unicum, quem Deum Deorum tanquam summum & optimum proprie nominare queas. Apud Orig. contra Cels. lib. 8. Hierocl. in carm. Pythag. pag. 10.
pass_a_gloss: Hence it is that Celsus in Origen affirms that he who venerates many Gods, by this very thing, inasmuch as he worships some one subject to the greatest God, does a thing pleasing to the highest God: and he adds, That it is lawful to follow no one with honor except whom he wills to be honored: wherefore he who venerates his subjects does not offend him whose all are. And therefore he wills those lower powers under the highest God to be worshipped so, That God be in no manner ever abandoned, not by night, not by day, not in private, not in public, not in any thoughts, not in works, but whether with these or without these the soul be always intent toward God. And afterwards, Thus, he says, you will seem to venerate the great God more, if you honor these also with hymns and praises. With which agrees what Hierocles teaches, that the Gods are to be acknowledged and worshipped as they are distinct from their author and parent, but their dignity is not to be raised beyond measure; finally that worship is to be referred to their one maker, whom you may properly name God of Gods as highest and best. In Origen, Against Celsus book 8. Hierocles on the Pythagorean verses page 10.
pass_b_english: This is why Celsus, as Origen reports him, says that whoever venerates many gods does something pleasing to the supreme God by that very act, insofar as he worships one who is subject to the greatest God. He adds: "No one may be honored except those whom God wills to be honored; so whoever venerates his subjects does not offend him to whom all belong."

So he wants the lesser powers under the supreme God to be worshiped in such a way "that God is never in any way abandoned, not by night, not by day, not in private, not in public, not in any thought, not in any work, but that with these or without them the soul is always intent on God." Later he says: "In this way you will seem to venerate the great God the more, if you honor these too with hymns and praises." (Origen, Against Celsus, book 8.)

With this agrees what Hierocles teaches: "The gods are to be acknowledged and worshiped as distinct from their author and parent, but their dignity is not to be raised beyond measure; in the end their worship is to be referred to their one maker, whom you may properly call the God of gods, as supreme and best." (Hierocles, On the Pythagorean Verses, page 10.)
